q: Where should you fire the engine to raise the far side of your orbit the most?
options: At the closest point to Earth
explain: You move fastest at the closest point (perigee), so the same push adds the most energy there. This is called the Oberth effect.

q: Which rocket launched Chandrayaan-3?
explain: ISRO's LVM3 rocket launched Chandrayaan-3 from Sriharikota on 14 July 2023.

q: About how far away is the Moon?
explain: On average the Moon is about 384,400 km away. Light takes about 1.3 seconds to cross that gap.

q: How long did Chandrayaan-3 take from launch to lunar orbit?
explain: Launched on 14 July, it entered lunar orbit on 5 August 2023: 22 days. Raising the orbit step by step saves fuel. Apollo needed the giant Saturn V to get there in 3 days.

q: Why must a spacecraft brake to go into orbit around the Moon?
options: It arrives too fast for the Moon's gravity to hold it
explain: Without braking you would swing past the Moon and fly away. Slowing down at the closest point lets the Moon's gravity capture you.

q: How strong is gravity on the Moon compared with Earth?
explain: The Moon's surface gravity is 1.62 m/s², about one-sixth of Earth's 9.81 m/s².

q: Where on the Moon did Vikram land?
explain: Vikram landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, the first landing ever in that region.

q: What name was given to Vikram's landing spot?
explain: It is called Shiv Shakti Point. Chandrayaan-2's impact site is Tiranga Point, and Chandrayaan-1's probe hit Jawahar Point.

q: Why can't a Moon lander use a parachute?
explain: A parachute needs air to push against. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so only rocket engines can slow you down.

q: How often do Earth and Mars line up for a fuel-saving trip?
explain: Earth laps Mars about every 780 days (26 months). That's when launch windows open.

q: How long did Mangalyaan take to fly from Earth to Mars?
explain: It left Earth orbit on 1 December 2013 and reached Mars on 24 September 2014, almost 300 days later.

q: Which country was the first to reach Mars orbit on its first try?
explain: India's Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, on the country's first attempt.

q: Mangalyaan was famous for being…
explain: The mission cost about ₹450 crore (roughly US$74 million), famously less than the budget of the film Gravity.

q: Why is a Mars landing called 'seven minutes of terror'?
options: Radio signals take minutes to reach Earth, so it must land all by itself
explain: Entry, parachute and landing take about 7 minutes, but radio needs several minutes to reach Earth. By the time we hear it started, it's already over.

q: What lowered Perseverance gently onto Mars?
explain: A rocket-powered sky crane hovered and lowered the rover on 6.4 m cables, then flew away.

q: How thick is Mars' air compared with Earth's?
explain: Surface pressure on Mars is about 0.6% to 1% of Earth's. Parachutes help, but they can't land you alone.

q: How does a gravity assist speed up a spacecraft?
options: It borrows a tiny bit of the planet's orbital motion
Its engines fire near the planet
explain: Passing behind a moving planet, the craft gets pulled along and gains speed. The planet slows by an immeasurably tiny amount.

q: Which is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune?
explain: Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, after Jupiter and Saturn.

q: In which year was Voyager 2 launched?
explain: Voyager 2 launched on 20 August 1977. It is still sending data from interstellar space.

q: What did Vikram do on 3 September 2023, after landing?
options: It hopped about 40 cm and landed again
explain: Vikram fired its engines, rose about 40 cm and landed 30–40 cm away, showing it could lift off again from the Moon.

q: Why was the hop important for future missions?
options: Missions that bring Moon samples back must lift off from the Moon
explain: Future sample-return and crewed missions must take off from the Moon. The hop proved the engines could restart there.

q: What went wrong on Apollo 13?
explain: An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon. The landing was cancelled and the crew flew around the Moon and home.

q: What happens if a capsule enters the air too shallowly?
options: It can skip off the atmosphere back into space
explain: Too shallow and it bounces off the top of the atmosphere, like a stone skipping on water. Too steep and it overheats.

q: Which spacecraft did the Apollo 13 crew use as a lifeboat?
explain: The crew moved into the Lunar Module Aquarius and used its engine and supplies to get home.

q: How fast must something go to escape Earth's gravity from its surface?
explain: Escape speed at Earth's surface is about 11.2 km/s, roughly 40,000 km/h. Higher up it is a little less.

q: Why did Mangalyaan circle Earth for almost a month before leaving?
options: Its rocket was small, so it raised its orbit step by step
explain: The PSLV rocket put it in an Earth orbit. Mangalyaan then fired its engine at perigee several times to build up speed before escaping.

q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
explain: Mercury orbits closest to the Sun, at about 58 million km.

q: Which is the largest planet?
explain: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.

q: What is the Sun?
explain: The Sun is a star: a giant ball of hot gas powered by nuclear fusion.

q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
explain: Light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to travel the 150 million km from the Sun.

q: Who was the first human in space?
explain: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth on 12 April 1961.

q: Who was the first Indian in space?
explain: Rakesh Sharma flew on a Soviet Soyuz in April 1984.

q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
explain: Iron oxide (rust) in its dust makes Mars look red.

q: How many planets are in our Solar System?
explain: There are eight planets. Pluto has been classed as a dwarf planet since 2006.

q: What was India's first satellite?
explain: Aryabhata was launched on 19 April 1975 by a Soviet rocket.

q: Where is India's main rocket launch centre?
explain: The Satish Dhawan Space Centre is at Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh.

q: Which is the hottest planet?
explain: Venus's thick carbon-dioxide air traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury.

q: What does a light-year measure?
explain: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year: about 9.5 trillion km.

q: What keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth?
explain: Earth's gravity keeps pulling the Moon, so it keeps falling around us instead of flying off.

q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
explain: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969 (21 July in UTC).

q: Which is the largest moon in the Solar System?
explain: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is even bigger than the planet Mercury.

q: What does Aditya-L1 study?
explain: Aditya-L1 watches the Sun from the L1 point, 1.5 million km from Earth.

q: About how fast must you go to stay in orbit just above Earth?
explain: About 7.8 km/s, roughly 28,000 km/h. Fast enough that you keep falling around the curve of Earth.

q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
options: It spins once for every orbit
explain: The Moon is tidally locked: it turns once on its axis each time it orbits Earth.

q: Which planet has the biggest, brightest rings?
explain: Saturn's rings are made of ice and rock, from tiny grains to house-sized chunks.

q: What do astronauts feel in orbit?
explain: Gravity is still about 90% as strong in low orbit. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling together.

q: Which mission took the famous 'Earthrise' photo?
explain: Apollo 8, the first crewed flight around the Moon, in December 1968.

q: What was the Apollo 11 lunar module called?
explain: The lunar module was Eagle; the command module that stayed in orbit was Columbia.

q: Which rocket gave India its first satellite launch from Indian soil?
explain: SLV-3 put Rohini into orbit on 18 July 1980.

q: What did Cassini drop onto Saturn's moon Titan?
explain: The European Huygens probe landed on Titan in January 2005: the farthest landing ever made.

q: What is the Moon Impact Probe's crash site called?
explain: Chandrayaan-1's probe hit near Shackleton crater on 14 November 2008, at Jawahar Point.

q: What shape is the famous bright region on Pluto?
explain: The heart-shaped plain is called Tombaugh Regio, after Pluto's discoverer Clyde Tombaugh.

q: Juno is named after a goddess who could see through…
explain: In myth, Juno saw through the clouds Jupiter hid behind. The spacecraft also peers beneath Jupiter's clouds.

q: How many satellites did PSLV-C37 launch in one flight?
explain: 104 satellites on 15 February 2017, a world record at the time.

q: Why is docking in space tricky?
options: Nothing slows you down, so you must brake yourself
explain: With no air, a spacecraft keeps moving at the same speed until its thrusters change it. That's Newton's first law.
